citation: Mattila P, Kumpulainen J. Coenzymes Q9 and Q10: contents in foods and dietary intake. J Food Compost Anal. 2001;14(4):409-17, Table 1
reproduced-in: Sadovska A, Bencko V. Nourishing and health benefits of coenzyme Q10. Czech J Food Sci. 2008;26(4):229-41, Table 1, which reprints Mattila and Kumpulainen's food table in full
unit: ug/g fresh weight, as the source prints it
to-page-unit: x0.1 gives mg/100 g, which is what coq9 and coq10 are stored in here
note: The first food table to carry CoQ9 as well as CoQ10, and still the only one reaching this page's vegetables and fruit. n.d. is the source's own mark for not detected; it publishes no limit of detection, so an absence here is weaker than Jensen's below-LOQ results but is still an assay that looked.
why-not-attested: Not wired into loadAttested, unlike the Jensen and Walther corpora. This is the Czech review's reprint rather than the 2001 original, and it is shorter than the original's 35 foods. Wiring a partial reproduction would fail every cell citing Mattila for a food the reprint omits, and one exists: sesame oil carries CoQ10 3.15 mg/100 g cited to Mattila, and this table's only dietary fat is rapeseed oil. A check that cannot tell a missing row from a wrong figure is worse than no check, so the figures are recorded and the cells stay unchecked with the other single-paper cells.
omitted: The meat, fish, egg and dairy rows of Table 1 are not transcribed. The page will never carry them, which is the same reason jensen-2025-vitamin-k.json keeps only its plant rows.

rows.note: The source states no preparation for any vegetable, so a cooked page food is close rather than exact.

rows.why-unmapped: The table says only "Bean". This page carries twenty of them and the row cannot be told which, so it reaches none. Kept because the figure is real and a later edition of the source may name the species.
Not a food on this page.
Not a food on this page. The richest plant source of CoQ9 in the table after the breads.

The page carries no bread. Kept for the same reason jensen-2025-vitamin-k.json keeps its bread rows: rye bread is the richest CoQ9 source in the table and the poorest in CoQ10, which is the whole point of the column, and it would arrive with menaquinones already measured.

rows.note: The source states no refining grade. Its CoQ10 of 6.35 mg/100 g is not the 3.5 the page carries from Fine 2016, which is a disagreement between two papers rather than an error in either, so only the CoQ9 absence is taken.
